name: Goal Gradient Effect
description: Effort and motivation toward a goal accelerate as perceived proximity to completion increases — including when that proximity is artificially pre-endowed rather than earned.
design_relevance_note: The direct theoretical basis for progress bars, pre-filled loyalty-card stamps, and completion-percentage indicators in onboarding flows.
myth_risk_note: Previously rated low because of 'limited evidence for recent direct replications or meta-analyses.' Resolved: Nunes & Dreze (2006) is a genuinely independent, contemporaneous confirmation of the same core mechanism via a different paradigm -- not a meta-analysis, but the strongest form of single-study corroboration (independent discovery, not a follow-up citing the original). The context-dependency caveat from the prior note (progress framing effects vary by context) remains a real, undisputed nuance, not a reason to doubt the core effect exists.
prevalence_note: A standard, widely-cited pattern in gamification and loyalty-program design specifically, though not as universally known outside that niche as e.g. anchoring or loss aversion.

findings.description: Customers who received a 12-stamp coffee card with 2 preexisting 'bonus' stamps already filled in completed their 10 required purchases faster than customers who received a plain 10-stamp card requiring the same 10 purchases — a manufactured sense of head-start progress accelerated behavior even though the actual remaining effort was identical, directly relevant to progress-bar and onboarding-checklist design that starts users with pre-filled steps.
findings.source_title: The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected: Purchase Acceleration, Illusionary Goal Progress, and Customer Retention

findings.description: In a real cafe loyalty reward program, participants purchased coffee more frequently the closer they were to earning a free coffee — a field-experiment demonstration of the goal-gradient effect in real consumer purchasing behavior, not just a lab artifact.
findings.source_title: The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected: Purchase Acceleration, Illusionary Goal Progress, and Customer Retention

applications.title: Been app discouraging users with an unrealistic 195-country travel goal
applications.description: The Been travel-tracking app displayed a goal of visiting all 195 countries immediately after a user logged their very first country, showing 0% progress toward that target -- rather than motivating continued use, the enormous, distant goal is presented as discouraging rather than energizing.
applications.ethical_note: A design-effectiveness failure with no persuasion or manipulation angle at all -- showing an unrealistic goal is a motivational misfire, not a dishonest or exploitative pattern.

applications.title: Blinkist showing a trial's first step as already completed to boost motivation
applications.description: In a redesigned trial flow, Blinkist added a visual 'first step (completed)' indicator to the onboarding timeline, signaling that the user's journey toward the trial's goal had already begun -- intended to increase motivation to finish by making the goal feel closer than a blank starting point would.
applications.ethical_note: Showing genuine progress the user has actually made (they did complete a real first step) is an honest motivational nudge, not a fabricated sense of advancement -- a clean contrast with the same case study's earlier hidden-close-button variant, which the redesign apparently moved away from.
